questions.q: A route does const updated = { ...user, ...body } with the client's JSON body. What is this bug called, and what can an attacker do with it?
questions.explain: Spreading an untrusted body copies every field it contains. Adding "role":"admin" to a profile edit turns a customer into an admin. Parse the body into a DTO with an allow-list of fields instead.
options: SQL injection: they can run their own SQL
Mass assignment: they can set fields they should never control, such as role
Cross-site scripting: they can run scripts in other users' browsers
A race condition: two updates can overwrite each other

questions.q: Why is type UserResponse = Omit<User, "passwordHash"> risky for a response type?
questions.explain: Omit means "everything except". When someone adds resetTokenHash to the entity next month, it is in the response without anyone deciding so. A response type that names its fields is an allow-list.
options: Omit does not work on interfaces
It makes every field optional
It is a deny-list: any field added to User later is published automatically
It removes passwordHash at compile time but not from the type

questions.q: In the lesson's BookStore, where does a new user's role come from at registration?
questions.explain: CreateUserDTO has no role, the parser refuses the key, and UserService.register writes role: "customer" itself. Admins are created by operators, never through the public API.
options: From the role field of the request body, if present
From the database's default value only
From the service, which always sets "customer"; a body with role is refused
From the token the client sends

questions.q: An update DTO has displayName?: string | null. What do "the key is absent" and "the key is null" mean?
questions.explain: A partial update must tell "not mentioned" from "set to nothing". The parser only sets the property when the key is in the body, and the SQL uses a flag so that NULL is written only when it was asked for.
options: Both mean "clear the name"
Both mean "leave the name alone"
Absent means "leave it alone"; null means "clear it"
Absent is an error; null means "leave it alone"

questions.q: A client sends {"title":"Kindred","id":7} to update a book. Why does the lesson answer 400 instead of silently ignoring id?
questions.explain: Silently dropping fields hides bugs in clients ("why does my id change never stick?") and hides probing. Refusing unknown keys, with a clear issue, is safer and easier to debug.
options: Because ignoring fields is impossible in TypeScript
A confused client learns about its mistake, and an attack attempt is visible instead of quietly half-working
Because PostgreSQL would reject the id anyway
Because a 400 is faster to send than a 200

questions.q: Which layer should enforce "only admins may change a book's price"?
questions.explain: The rule depends on who is asking, which the parser does not know, and it is a business rule, which the repository should not know. The service sees the principal and the request, and every caller (HTTP, scripts, jobs) goes through it.
options: The DTO parser
The response mapper
The service
The repository

questions.q: Which layer turns the column price_cents into the property priceCents?
questions.explain: Only the repository knows column names. Its private row type and toBook mapper keep snake_case inside the database layer, so no other code changes when a column is renamed.
options: The controller
The DTO parser
The repository's row mapper
The service

questions.q: A request to create a book arrives with a valid token for a customer. Which status is right?
questions.explain: 401 means "we don't know who you are" (authentication failed). 403 means "we know who you are, and the answer is no" (authorization failed). The customer is authenticated, so it is 403.
options: 401 Unauthorized, because the customer is not allowed
403 Forbidden: we know who they are, and they may not do this
404 Not Found, because books are not theirs
400 Bad Request, because the body is wrong for a customer

questions.q: Why does the lesson put permission checks in the services instead of only in the controllers?
questions.explain: Put a rule where every path passes. A background job that calls BookService.update directly must be checked just like an HTTP request.
options: Controllers cannot throw errors
Services are also called from admin scripts, queue jobs and tests; a check in the controller protects only the HTTP door
Services run faster than controllers
TypeScript does not allow imports of the policy in controllers

questions.q: The Authenticator reads only the user id from the token and loads the user to get the role. What does that buy you?
questions.explain: A role copied into a token is a snapshot. Loading the user each time costs one query but always uses the current role. (Signing, not loading, is what makes a token unforgeable.)
options: Tokens become shorter, which is the main goal
Nothing: putting the role in the token would be the same
Role changes take effect on the next request; a demoted admin does not keep admin rights until the token expires
It makes the token impossible to forge

questions.q: Why do the services receive a Clock instead of calling new Date()?
questions.explain: The current time is an input from outside, like a database. Injecting it lets a test say "it is 10:00" and check the result exactly.
options: Because new Date() is not allowed in services
So tests and demos can fix the time, and outputs such as createdAt are the same on every run
Because Clock is faster than Date
So the database can set the time instead

questions.q: Which sentence describes dependency inversion in the lesson's code?
questions.explain: The high-level code states what it needs as an interface (a port). The low-level code fits that interface. The composition root connects them, which is why a test can pass a fake.
options: The repository imports the service and calls it
The service depends on a BookRepository interface, and the PGlite repository implements it; neither imports the other
The service creates its own PgBookRepository in its constructor
Every class depends on app.ts

questions.q: Why does BookService.list ask the repository for limit + 1 rows?
questions.explain: The extra row is only a probe. The page shows limit items; nextCursor is set only when the probe row came back. Counting a large table for every page would be much slower.
options: To make up for an off-by-one error in SQL LIMIT
If the extra row exists, there is a next page, so it knows whether to return a cursor without a COUNT(*) query
To return one bonus item to the client
Because PostgreSQL skips the first row of every page

questions.q: The cursor is a base64url string the server created itself. Why does parsePageQuery still validate it?
questions.explain: Anything that arrives in a request is client input, even if you generated it earlier. An unchecked cursor could become a SQL error, a crash or a way to read unexpected rows.
options: Because base64url decoding is slow
It doesn't need to; the server wrote it
It comes back from the client, who can send any string, so it is untrusted input like every other query parameter
Because cursors expire after one hour

questions.q: What does as const satisfies Record<Failure["kind"], number> on the STATUS table guarantee?
questions.explain: satisfies checks the object against the type without widening it. Adding a new kind to Failure without a status becomes a compile error pointing at this table.
options: That every status is between 400 and 599
That every failure kind has a status, while TypeScript keeps the exact literal numbers
That the table can be changed at runtime
That no two kinds share a status

questions.q: A controller promises ApiResponse<UserResponse> and returns { status: 200, body: user }, where user is the entity with a passwordHash. When does this compile?
questions.explain: TypeScript is structural: an object with more properties fits a type with fewer. Excess-property errors only apply to fresh object literals. In the lesson, only the Date vs string mismatch stopped it; an explicit mapper is the real protection.
options: Never: TypeScript forbids extra fields on assignment
Whenever every field of UserResponse has a matching type on User, because extra fields are allowed on a variable
Only with strict turned off
Only if passwordHash is optional

questions.q: Ada asks for GET /users/3, another customer's private profile. Why might you answer 404 instead of 403?
questions.explain: The difference between 403 and 404 leaks information. For private resources, "you may not see it" and "it does not exist" should look the same to the caller.
options: Because 404 responses are cached
A 403 confirms that user 3 exists; answering 404 for "exists but hidden" and "does not exist" stops id probing
Because 403 is only for administrators
Because the service cannot throw a forbidden error there

questions.q: toErrorResponse receives an error that is not an AppError. What does it do, and why?
questions.explain: An unexpected error is your bug, not the client's mistake. Its message can reveal SQL, paths or internals. Log it for yourself; tell the client only that something went wrong.
options: Returns the error's message and stack with status 400, to help the client
Logs it on the server and returns a bare 500, because it is a bug and its details must not reach the client
Retries the request
Converts it to a validation failure

questions.q: What is special about createApp in src/app.ts?
questions.explain: This is the composition root. Services and controllers only know interfaces and each other's types; swapping PGlite for a PostgreSQL server, or scrypt for another hasher, changes this file only.
options: It contains all the business rules
It is the only file that may import types
It is the one place that knows every concrete class, creates them and connects them
It is loaded again for every request

questions.q: The unit test gives BookService an in-memory fake repository. Which mistake can that test not catch?
questions.explain: The fake replaces the SQL, so the SQL is not exercised. Rules and paging logic are tested fast with the fake; the repository needs its own integration test against a real database.
options: A customer being allowed to create books
A page that skips an item
A typo in the SQL of PgBookRepository
A missing nextCursor on the last page

questions.q: Why does the user repository check the row's role with isRole before building the entity?
questions.explain: The row type can only honestly say string. The guard turns it into "customer" | "admin" with proof, so a bad row fails loudly at the edge instead of confusing permission checks later.
options: Because PostgreSQL returns roles in upper case
The column arrives as a plain string; the entity claims Role, and the database is outside data too
Because the CHECK constraint does not work in PGlite
To make the query faster

questions.q: Why is ApiResponse generic (ApiResponse<T>) instead of having body: unknown?
questions.explain: Promise<ApiResponse<Page<BookResponse>>> documents and checks the endpoint's contract. With body: unknown, anything would compile.
options: Generic types are required for JSON
Each controller method states what it sends, so returning the wrong shape is a compile error and readers see the contract in the signature
So the response can hold several bodies
Because unknown cannot be serialized

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The cast silences the compiler, and the spread copies every field of the body, including role. That is mass assignment.
options: customer Ada Obi
admin Ada Obi
customer Ada
It does not compile

questions.q: A new field was added to the entity. What does this mapper publish?
questions.explain: The rest spread keeps everything it was not told to remove. The two-factor secret leaks without any change to the mapper: the danger of a deny-list.
options: [ 'id', 'email' ]
[ 'id', 'email', 'twoFactorSecret' ]
[ 'id', 'email', 'passwordHash', 'twoFactorSecret' ]

questions.q: The function's parameter type has only two fields. What does it print?
questions.explain: Types are erased at runtime; they never remove properties. And user is a variable, not a fresh literal, so the extra field compiles. Only a mapper that builds a new object stops the leak.
options: {"id":2,"email":"ada@example.com"}
{"id":2,"email":"ada@example.com","passwordHash":"scrypt$x$y"}
It does not compile: passwordHash is not in UserResponse

questions.q: A partial update is applied with a spread. What does it print?
questions.explain: A property that is present with the value undefined still overwrites. Partial allows that unless exactOptionalPropertyTypes is on. This is why parsers should only set keys that were really sent.
options: { title: 'Kindred (2nd ed.)', stock: 4 }
{ title: 'Kindred (2nd ed.)', stock: undefined }
{ title: 'Kindred', stock: 4 }
It does not compile

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With in, the property is only set when the key was sent. "Not sent" stays absent, null stays null, and a string is trimmed.

questions.q: This is the service's paging logic with 5 stored ids. What does it print?
questions.explain: The repository returns up to limit + 1 rows. The page shows limit of them, and the next cursor points after the last one shown, id 2. After id 4 only one row exists, so there is no next page.
options:
{ items: [ 1, 2 ], next: 3 }
{ items: [ 5 ], next: 5 }

{ items: [ 1, 2 ], next: 2 }
{ items: [ 5 ], next: null }

{ items: [ 1, 2, 3 ], next: 3 }
{ items: [ 5 ], next: null }

{ items: [ 1, 2 ], next: 2 }
{ items: [ 5 ], next: 5 }

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: base64url has no = padding. Decoding checks the exact format: random text fails, and so does a negative id, because the pattern only accepts digits.
options:
YWZ0ZXI6Mg 2
invalid -1

YWZ0ZXI6Mg 2
invalid invalid

after:2 2
invalid invalid

YWZ0ZXI6Mg== 2
invalid invalid

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each kind looks up its own status. Forbidden (known user, not allowed) is 403; unauthenticated (unknown user) is 401.
options: [ 'forbidden', 'unauthenticated', 'validation' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each role has an explicit list of actions. Anything not granted is refused: a customer may read their own orders but not create books.
options: true true true
false true true
false false true
false true false

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify calls Date.prototype.toJSON, which gives an ISO string (months count from 0, so 8 is September). After parsing, it is only a string. That is why the response DTO types createdAt as string, not Date.
options:
{"id":1,"createdAt":{}}
object

{"id":1,"createdAt":1790244000000}
number

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Missing allowed keys are fine (an update may send only some). Every key outside the allow-list is reported, so both id and authorId are refused.
options:
[ 'title cannot be set' ]
[ 'id cannot be set' ]

[]
[ 'id cannot be set', 'authorId cannot be set' ]

[]
[ 'id cannot be set' ]

[ 'stock cannot be set' ]
[ 'id cannot be set', 'authorId cannot be set' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Inside each case, TypeScript narrows failure to that member of the union, so failure.id and failure.message are known to exist.
options:
not_found
conflict

No book with id 99
That e-mail is already registered

No book with id undefined
That e-mail is already registered
It does not compile: failure.id may not exist

questions.q: Write toUserResponse(user). It must name every field it publishes (no spreads), leave out passwordHash, and turn createdAt into an ISO string.
questions.explain: A new object built field by field is an allow-list: fields added to User later stay private until someone adds them here on purpose.

questions.q: Finish parseUpdateBook: allowed keys are title and stock. Every other key is an issue (KEY cannot be set), stock must be a whole number from 0 to 10000 (stock must be 0 to 10000), and only keys that were sent end up in the DTO. Throw an Error with the issues joined by "; ".
questions.explain: The allow-list refuses id, the range check refuses -1, and both are reported together. The first body only mentions stock, so the DTO has no title key at all.
questions.expected:
{"stock":4}
id cannot be set; stock must be 0 to 10000

questions.q: Write authorize(principal, action): throw Error("unauthenticated") when there is no principal, Error("forbidden: ACTION") when the role lacks the action, and return the principal otherwise.
questions.explain: Check authentication first (no principal: 401), then authorization (principal without the grant: 403). Returning the principal lets the caller continue with a value that is known to be allowed.
questions.expected:
allowed for user 1
forbidden: book:create
unauthenticated

questions.q: Write the generic toPage(rows, limit, idOf): rows holds up to limit + 1 items. Return { items, nextCursor } where items has at most limit items and nextCursor is "after:ID" of the last shown item when an extra row exists, otherwise null.
questions.explain: The cursor points after the last item shown (id 7), not after the probe row (id 9); otherwise the next page would skip a book. idOf keeps the function generic over any item type.
questions.expected:
{"items":[{"id":4,"title":"Kindred"},{"id":7,"title":"Arrow of God"}],"nextCursor":"after:7"}
{"items":[{"id":9,"title":"Half of a Yellow Sun"}],"nextCursor":null}

questions.q: Write the STATUS table so that every failure kind maps to its HTTP status, checked with satisfies Record<Failure["kind"], number>: validation 400, unauthenticated 401, forbidden 403, not_found 404, conflict 409.
questions.explain: Typed as Record<string, number>, the table accepts any key and misses none. With satisfies Record<Failure["kind"], number>, a new failure kind without a status is a compile error.

questions.q: Write toBook(row) that maps a database row with snake_case columns to the Book entity.
questions.explain: The row type describes the database, the entity describes your code, and this mapper is the only place that knows both. Renaming a column later means changing the row type and this one function.
questions.expected: { id: 1, title: 'Things Fall Apart', authorId: 1, priceCents: 1299 }

questions.q: Write applyChanges(book, changes) that copies only the change keys whose value is not undefined, so { stock: undefined } leaves the stock alone.
questions.explain: A spread copies a key even when its value is undefined. Taking each field with ?? is the JavaScript version of SQL's COALESCE(new, old). It only works because neither field may be null; a nullable field needs the "was it sent?" flag from the lesson.

questions.q: Write MemoryBookRepository, a fake that implements BookRepository with an array, so the service below can run without a database.
questions.explain: restock only knows the interface, so a small real implementation in memory is enough to test it. implements BookRepository makes the compiler check that the fake keeps the port's contract.
questions.expected:
Kindred: 4 in stock
book 2 not found
